source.title: ForeCite: Adapting Pre-Trained Language Models to Predict Future Citation Rates of Academic Papers

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how a downstream prediction metric changes with model size and data volume, but uses citation-prediction correlation rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior scaling-law work and reports its own downstream scaling experiment. The citation-prediction results bear on V6, but do not measure pretraining loss, validate an actual larger-run extrapolation, or test compute-optimal allocation. Temporal holdout, saliency, title/abstract ablations, and pretraining ablations do not measure a version's named scaling outcome; cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes five off-the-shelf LMs (0.56B–14.8B) on 1–16% of a citation-regression corpus and reports held-out test correlations across the full grid. That is a new downstream setting bearing on V6: does downstream performance improve predictably with scale? It measures no pretraining loss and controls no pretraining runs. The 'data' axis is fine-tuning data, not pretraining tokens.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that citation-prediction performance grows predictably with parameter count and data volume: monotonically with data, more aberrantly with model size. They attribute the mid-sized deviations to prior specialised fine-tuning of Phi-4-mini-instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-7B. They also conclude that reasoning fine-tuning does not help and may slightly hurt. Their tanh-log fit extrapolates to r≈0.94 for a 288B model on the full corpus.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream citation-rate regression task using a linear head and QLoRA fine-tuning, evaluated by prediction correlations; it is not a language-model pretraining loss scaling experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Data volume changes performance; the authors report mid-sized-model deviations and differences between original and reasoning-distilled checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: Randomly re-initialised Llama-3.2-1B performs far worse than the pretrained model; the gap narrows from Δr=0.617 to 0.313 as fine-tuning data grows (Appendix I).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining benefit on downstream fine-tuning shrinks as fine-tuning data grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Reasoning-distilled Qwen2.5 checkpoints slightly underperform their originals at ≥4% data (Appendix G, Fig. 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prior specialised fine-tuning reduces downstream transfer independent of scale.

record.code_released: Relevant code and checkpoints are stated to be made available upon publication; no URL is given.
record.problems: The study reports single-run experiments and no uncertainty estimates. Data use is limited to 1%–16% of the corpus; the proposed large-model result is an extrapolation rather than an observed run. The measured outcome is citation-prediction correlation, not held-out pretraining loss. The text also describes data fractions as 1%–16% and approximately 90K–144K articles, without reconciling those quantities with the stated corpus size.
record.rows_left_out: Train-split metrics in Appendix D, Table 8 were excluded because the claim version tested here concerns downstream predictability and the held-out test metrics are the relevant results. The Llama 4 Behemoth estimate in Section 4.1 and Figure 4 is not an observed model result. The temporal-holdout results in Section 4.3/Figure 5 and the title/abstract ablations in Appendix H/Figure 12 do not test the listed scaling versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining cross-entropy is measured; the models are off-the-shelf with no controlled pretraining.
The 288B 'Llama 4 Behemoth' value is an unverified extrapolation of a tanh-log fit; no larger run is evaluated.
Shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count.
The fine-tuning-data trend is measured as correlation, not loss, and no power law is fitted (the fit is tanh of log-linear), so power-law form is not tested.
There is no relation to pretraining loss, and model size is confounded with model family and prior fine-tuning.
There is no comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Fitted tanh(β0+β1 log2 p+β2 log2 d) parameters (r: 0.6771, 0.0689, 0.0767) with MAE ≈0.03. This is the authors' 'predictable' functional form, not a power law.
Spearman ρ, R², MSE and MAE for the test split across the 25-cell grid; these show the same trends as r.

record.verdict_notes: The model-size comparison is across different families, pretraining corpora and post-training stages, so it is a weak test of size scaling. The data axis is fine-tuning data (≈90K–144K articles per the table caption, which is inconsistent with 1%–16% of 900K+). All runs are single, with no uncertainty reported. Gains with data shrink for larger models: Qwen2.5-14B rises only 0.826→0.844 from 4% to 16%.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute.
The estimated 288B-model result is an extrapolation, not an evaluation of a run orders of magnitude larger than the fitted runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
Architecture shape, including depth and width, is not varied at fixed parameter count.
The study is a biomedical-text citation-prediction task; it does not test power-law form across modalities or other training regimes.
No relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is tested; the downstream task is citation-rate prediction.
The study does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices. Its mid-sized-model deviations concern downstream correlation, not cross-entropy scaling curves.

relationships.condition: Fine-tuning data volume 1%→16%, test split, all five models
relationships.reason: Test r rises monotonically with data for every model, e.g. Bloom 0.430→0.721 (r01–r05) and Qwen2.5-14B 0.752→0.844 (r21–r25).
relationships.display_finding: Test correlations increased at every data step for every model, including Bloom from 0.430 to 0.721 and Qwen2.5-14B from 0.752 to 0.844.

relationships.condition: Model-size axis across heterogeneous model families, mid-sized models (1B–8B)
relationships.reason: Size trends are non-monotonic. At 1% data, 1.24B (0.674) beats 3.84B (0.657) and 7.62B (0.645) (r06, r11, r16). At 16%, 7.62B (0.786) is below 3.84B (0.802) (r15, r20). The authors call these 'noticeable deviations'.
relationships.display_finding: At 1% data, the 1.24B model scored 0.674 versus 0.657 for 3.84B and 0.645 for 7.62B; at 16% data, 7.62B scored 0.786, below 3.84B's 0.802.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Test-set citation-prediction performance as training data increases from 1% to 16%, across the five models in Table 8
reader_labels.reason: Pearson correlation increases monotonically with data fraction for every listed model; rows r01-r25 show the reported grid.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The authors report noticeable mid-sized-model deviations, and state that the original Qwen2.5 variants outperform distilled counterparts at 4% and above; the latter comparison is figure-only. Rows r06-r25 and r26-r35 record the relevant results.
